content.title: Johns Hopkins researchers want to clear up mRNA vaccine misconceptions that began during COVID
content.text: There's renewed debate on the future of mRNA vaccines, and Johns Hopkins researchers want to clear up some misconceptions around the shots.The mRNA vaccines gained attention during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, though the technology is far from new.The vaccines are replicating vaccines, so they use synthetic molecules rather than a live virus. It teaches the body's immune cells how to make antigens to fight the disease. Unlike other vaccines, they can be made in a matter of months."It's sort of like switching from a horse and buggy to a Corvette for travel," said Dr. Andrew Pekosz, with the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. "The mRNA still does the basic thing, just a lot faster."That's why researchers want to use the technology for flu shots. Currently, health agencies make predictions in February on what they think will be the dominant flu strain in September.However, sometimes the predictions aren't accurate. Doses of mRNA could improve the efficacy."mRNA vaccines can make flu vaccines more effective than (they are) currently, and better matched against the viruses that we're all likely to be exposed to in the flu season," said Dr. Gigi Gronvall, with the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.Researchers are also targeting mRNA technology for cancer vaccines. Because mRNA doses can be made quickly, they could become a source of personalized treatments."Much of this technology is in its early stages of development," Pekosz said. "But it's really fascinating to think one could design this kind of personalized medicine relatively quickly, and then hopefully boost the efficacy (with) which these treatments can work on an individual basis."Recent studies have shown mRNA does not cause fertility problems in women.
